screens.title: If, Elif, Else — Conditional Tests
screens.narratorSegment: Conditional statements let your script make decisions based on file properties, string contents, numeric comparisons, or the exit status of commands. The basic if structure reads a condition and runs the then-block when the condition is true. Use the single-bracket form with spaces: open square bracket, condition, close square bracket. For richer pattern matching and logical operators prefer double square brackets. Typical tests include file checks like -f and -d, string tests such as -z for empty or == for equality, and numeric comparisons using -eq, -ne, -lt and so on. A practical example: test whether a configuration file exists and, if not, create a default one and report the action. A common mistake is leaving out spaces around brackets or using = for numeric comparisons; those errors either produce syntax errors or incorrect results. You can also combine conditions using && for AND and || for OR inside double brackets, or chain tests with elif to express multiple branches. When checking a command that returns success or failure, a compact pattern is to negate the command with an exclamation mark so the condition becomes true on non-zero exit status. To check your understanding, try writing a conditional that verifies a directory is writable and prints an error if it is not. The core idea is that correct spacing, operator choice, and thought about command exit behavior are what make conditionals reliable.

keyIdea.title: Conditional checklist
keyIdea.text: Always use spaces with [ ] tests, choose operators appropriate to the data type, and prefer [[ ]] for complex expressions with && or ||.

content.html:
Core Concept › If / Elif / Else
Definition and Syntax
Use tests to evaluate conditions; run the then-block when true, otherwise use elif or else.
if [ -f "/path/to/file.txt" ]; then
  echo "File exists."
elif [[ -d "/some/dir" ]]; then
  echo "Directory exists."
else
  echo "Neither found."
fi
Common operators: -f, -d, -z, -n, ==, !=, -eq, -ne
Pitfall: Missing spaces around [ and ] causes syntax errors.
Example: Check and create config
Test for a file and create a default if missing to keep services working.
if [ ! -f "$HOME/.appconfig" ]; then cp /etc/app/default.conf "$HOME/.appconfig" echo "Default config created." fi
Key Takeaway

Write clear tests, use the right operator for data type, and prefer [[ ]] when combining conditions.

Common Mistake
Using = for numeric comparisons or omitting spaces inside [ ] yields wrong behavior or syntax errors.

screens.title: case Statement
screens.narratorSegment: The case statement provides a concise and readable way to select one action from many possible values. Instead of chaining many elif conditions, case compares a variable against several patterns and executes the commands for the first matching pattern. Patterns can include simple words or shell globs such as start|stop|restart. Always end each pattern block with a double semicolon to separate it from the next. Use an asterisk star pattern as the default branch, similar to else. A common use is processing command-line arguments where the user passes a verb like start, stop or restart; case keeps the logic clear and avoids repetitive string comparisons. For example, a service-control script can map start to systemctl start and restart to systemctl restart. A misconception is thinking case matches substrings — it matches patterns, so include anchors or globs as needed. Also remember to quote variables where expansions may be empty. After building a case-based menu, test unexpected inputs to ensure the default branch handles mistakes gracefully. Consider pairing case with functions so each branch calls a named function, improving readability and testability.

content.html:
Definition › case Statement
Syntax Example
Match an action argument and call the appropriate command.
case "$1" in
  start) systemctl start my_app.service ;;
  stop) systemctl stop my_app.service ;;
  restart) systemctl restart my_app.service ;;
  *) echo "Usage: start|stop|restart" ;;
esac
Practical tip
Group similar patterns with vertical bars and use the default branch to validate input.
Example Scenario
A maintenance script that accepts apply|rollback|status can use case to dispatch to named functions for each action.
Key Takeaway

Use case to keep multi-choice logic readable and pair branches with functions for clarity.

screens.title: for Loops
screens.narratorSegment: A for loop iterates over a set of items and runs the same commands for each item. This is ideal for processing files, applying transformations, or batching administrative tasks. The basic pattern iterates over words or glob expansions: for FILE in *. log; do process "$FILE"; done. When filenames include spaces, quote variables to preserve the name as a single item. You can also iterate over a numeric sequence using brace expansion or seq. A common example is compressing all rotated logs or changing ownership across many files. For loops are deterministic: the list is evaluated before the loop runs, so adding or removing files during iteration may not affect the current pass. A typical mistake is using for FILE in $(ls *. log) which breaks on whitespace; prefer globs or an array. Use continue to skip items and break to exit the loop early on a fatal condition. For clarity and reuse, factor the per-item work into a function and call it from inside the loop. That makes debugging easier and lets you test the action independently of the looping mechanism.

content.html:
Process Flow › for Loop
Loop pattern
Iterate over a glob or list and process each item. Quote variables to handle spaces.
for FILE in /var/log/*.log; do
  echo "Processing: $FILE"
  gzip "$FILE"
done
Avoid: for F in $(ls *.log); do — this breaks on whitespace. Use globs or arrays instead.
Example: Batch archive
Loop through found old logs and add them to an archive or process them one by one reliably.
Key Takeaway

Use clear iteration sources, quote expansions, and break work into functions for testable loops.

Common Mistake
Not quoting $FILE when names include spaces leads to multiple unintended items and broken behavior.

screens.title: while Loops
screens.narratorSegment: While loops run as long as a given condition evaluates to true. They are suited for reading streams, waiting for a condition, or processing input until an end-of-file. A common idiom reads lines from a file safely with IFS read -r inside a while loop and then redirects the file into the loop. This avoids subshell issues and preserves whitespace. For example: while IFS= read -r LINE; do echo "$LINE"; done < input. txt. Another pattern uses a boolean condition that checks command output or the existence of a file, updating state inside the loop until the condition becomes false. The primary risk with while loops is infinite loops if the condition never changes; always ensure loop progress or include a timeout counter. To stop early on error, check exit status inside the loop and break if necessary. A misconception is expecting while to be faster than for — performance depends on the work done inside the loop. Design your loop body to do minimal external calls when processing many items to keep it efficient. while Loops means ensure the loop condition progresses, prefer ifs read -r for line input, and add timeouts or counters to prevent infinite loops.. In practical terms, repeat until a condition changes or input ends. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › while Loop
Safe file reading
Read lines robustly and preserve spaces using IFS and read -r.
while IFS= read -r LINE; do
  echo "Line: $LINE"
done < input.txt
Add counters or timeouts if the loop watches a resource to avoid infinite loops.
Example: Polling with timeout
Poll a service and give up after N attempts to avoid hanging indefinitely.
attempts=0 while ! systemctl is-active --quiet my_app.service; do attempts=$((attempts+1)) if [ $attempts -gt 10 ]; then echo "Service failed to start" break fi sleep 2 done
Key Takeaway

Prefer while for streaming input or polling, and always ensure a termination condition or counter.

screens.title: Functions and Modularity
screens.narratorSegment: Functions let you group related commands into a named block that you can call with arguments. They make scripts easier to read and maintain, because you move repeated logic into a single place and give it a meaningful name. Define a function with function_name() { commands; } and call it by name. Inside the function use positional parameters like dollar sign one and dollar sign two to access passed arguments. Good practice is to return an exit status with return so callers can react based on success or failure. For example, create a function archive_file that takes a path, checks existence, appends it to the archive and returns non-zero on failure. This lets the main script call archive_file inside a loop and skip or retry on failure based on the returned status. A common misconception is that functions create a separate scope for variables — in POSIX shells, functions inherit and share the environment unless you explicitly use local to limit scope. Use local for temporary variables inside functions to avoid unintended side effects. Designing small, single-purpose functions improves testability and reduces the chance of bugs in large scripts.

keyIdea.title: Function design
keyIdea.text: Write small, single-purpose functions, use local variables, accept parameters, and return meaningful exit codes.

content.html:
Definition › Functions
Function example
Encapsulate archiving behavior in a testable unit that returns status.
archive_file() {
  local file="$1"
  if [ ! -f "$file" ]; then
    return 1
  fi
  tar -czf "$ARCHIVE" "$file" --remove-files || return 2
  return 0
}
Usage pattern
Call functions inside loops and check their return codes to decide next steps.
Key Takeaway

Functions keep scripts modular. Use local variables and return values to make code predictable and testable.

screens.title: Exit Status and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Every command in a shell returns an exit status: zero typically means success, and any non-zero value signals an error. Scripts should check these statuses to decide how to proceed. The special variable dollar sign question holds the exit status of the most recently executed command. A practical pattern is to test the return value immediately after a critical command and take action on failure, such as retrying, logging, or exiting with a clear status. For instance, after attempting to create an archive you might test dollar sign question and print an error and exit with a non-zero code if archiving failed. Another common approach is to write functions that return specific codes for different failure modes, allowing higher-level logic to react appropriately. A misconception is assuming that a command printed to the terminal means it succeeded; always check the exit status. Also be aware that pipelines return the exit status of the last command in some shells by default; use pipefail if you need to detect failures earlier in a pipeline. Robust scripts explicitly handle errors near the source and provide informative messages so scheduled jobs don't silently fail.

keyIdea.title: Check exit codes
keyIdea.text: Use $? after critical commands, and design functions to return meaningful non-zero codes for error handling and retries.

content.html:
Core Concept › Exit Status ($?)
Immediate check
Inspect $? right after a command to make branching decisions or to exit early on error.
cp source dest
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Copy failed" >&2
  exit 1
fi
Function-based errors
Return codes let callers react differently to specific failures.
Key Takeaway

Treat exit codes as contract values. Check them, log failures, and fail fast when the state is unsafe to continue.

screens.title: set -e and Script Safety
screens.narratorSegment: The set -e option causes a script to exit immediately when a command returns a non-zero status. This is a useful safety mechanism for preventing later commands from running after an earlier failure. Use it at the top of scripts that should not continue when a step has failed. However, set -e has caveats: it may exit in contexts you expect to handle errors, such as conditional checks whose failures are used deliberately. You can work around this by checking command status explicitly when you expect non-zero outcomes, or by using command lists with || true for tolerated failures. Another helpful option for pipelines is set -o pipefail which ensures the pipeline's exit status reflects the first failing command instead of the last. A common misconception is that set -e alone makes a script fully robust — it helps, but you still need explicit checks and clear return codes in functions. Test scripts with intentional failures to understand how set -e affects control flow. When combined with good logging and return codes, set -e reduces the risk of scripts continuing in a broken state and causing wider system issues.

You can work around this by checking command status explicitly when you expect non-zero outcomes, or by using command lists with || true for tolerated failures. When combined with good logging and return codes, set -e reduces the risk of scripts continuing in a broken state and causing wider system issues.

keyIdea.title: Use set -e carefully
keyIdea.text: set -e helps fail fast but requires explicit handling for expected non-zero commands and paired options like pipefail for pipelines.

content.html:
Process Flow › set -e
Safety example
Start scripts with set -e to stop on unexpected failures, but handle expected non-zero statuses explicitly.
#!/bin/bash set -e set -o pipefail # critical steps follow cp /important/file /backup/ # if cp fails, script exits automatically
When not to use it
If you deliberately expect a command to fail as part of a check, handle it with an if statement instead of relying on set -e behavior.
Key Takeaway

set -e reduces silent failures but pair it with explicit checks and pipefail to get predictable behavior in pipelines.

screens.title: Archive Logs Script + crontab Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a practical script that archives log files older than seven days and then schedule it with cron. The script starts with a shebang and set -e to enforce fail-fast behavior. It defines variables for the log and archive directories and ensures the archive directory exists. It then finds matching files older than seven days using find with -mtime +7 and writes the list to a temporary file. If the list is non-empty, the script creates a compressed archive with tar and removes originals, logging progress as it goes. Note the use of checks for directory existence and testing whether the temp file is empty to avoid running tar on an empty list. After testing locally, schedule the script using crontab -e. A correct crontab entry for daily 2:00 AM uses minute hour day month weekday fields: 0 2 * * * followed by the absolute script path and redirected output to a log file. For testing, schedule the job a minute or two in the future to confirm it runs and writes expected output. Common mistakes are forgetting full paths in cron or not redirecting stdout and stderr, which can lead to unexpected mailbox messages. This exercise ties conditionals, loops, functions and cron into a single, verifiable workflow.

Common mistakes are forgetting full paths in cron or not redirecting stdout and stderr, which can lead to unexpected mailbox messages. This exercise ties conditionals, loops, functions and cron into a single, verifiable workflow.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity › archive_logs.sh & crontab
Script (excerpt)
#!/bin/bash
# archive_logs.sh
set -e

LOG_DIR="$HOME/test_logs"
ARCHIVE_DIR="$HOME/archived_logs"
ARCHIVE_FILENAME="archive_$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz"
FULL_ARCHIVE_PATH="$ARCHIVE_DIR/$ARCHIVE_FILENAME"

# Create archive directory if missing
if [ ! -d "$ARCHIVE_DIR" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$ARCHIVE_DIR"
fi

OLD_LOGS=$(find "$LOG_DIR" -type f -name "*.log" -mtime +7)

if [ -z "$OLD_LOGS" ]; then
  echo "No log files older than 7 days found."
else
  TEMP_FILE_LIST=$(mktemp)
  echo "$OLD_LOGS" > "$TEMP_FILE_LIST"
  if [ -s "$TEMP_FILE_LIST" ]; then
    tar -czf "$FULL_ARCHIVE_PATH" -T "$TEMP_FILE_LIST" --remove-files
  fi
  rm -f "$TEMP_FILE_LIST"
fi
Crontab example
0 2 * * * /bin/bash $HOME/archive_logs.sh >> $HOME/archive_logs.log 2>&1
Testing tip
Schedule the job one or two minutes ahead to confirm it runs, then remove the entry after testing if needed.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we move from simple command sequences to scripts that make decisions, repeat work, handle errors, and run automatically. You will learn how to use conditionals to choose actions, use loops to process many items, and encapsulate logic in functions for reuse. We’ll also cover exit status checks and the safety option set -e so your scripts fail fast when something goes wrong. Finally, you’ll learn to schedule tasks with cron so scripts run without manual intervention. For example, you will build a log-archiving script that finds files older than seven days, packages them, deletes originals, and then schedule it to run nightly. Along the way we’ll highlight common pitfalls: missing spaces in if tests, accidental infinite loops, forgetting full paths in cron, and not checking exit codes. These techniques make shell scripting reliable and maintainable in real systems administration. After working through the examples and the hands-on activity, you’ll be ready to write scripts that act predictably under error conditions and that run on a schedule without surprises.

By the end of this chapter you will implement practical scripting techniques that automate routine tasks. You will write conditionals to make choices based on file tests or command output, and you will select the appropriate pattern — if/elif/else or case — when your logic needs multiple distinct branches. You will use for and while loops to process lists of files or to read input until a condition ends, and you will learn how to avoid infinite loops with proper loop control. You will design functions to encapsulate repeated logic, pass parameters, and return meaningful exit statuses for error handling. You will inspect and use exit codes to drive decisions inside scripts and apply set -e to make scripts fail fast when a command fails. Finally, you will schedule a script with cron, test it for a quick run, and ensure your job uses full paths and redirects output so cron behaves predictably. These objectives give you a repeatable workflow for building safe, modular, and scheduled automation.

This second objectives screen ties the chapter goals to a learning progression. First, you will learn to recognize and write conditional tests: file tests, string and numeric comparisons, and compound conditions. Next, you will apply loops to perform repeated actions and refactor repetitive code into functions for reuse and readability. After that, you will analyze command exit statuses and adopt safety practices such as checking $? and using set -e where appropriate. Finally, you will create scheduled automation with cron, test it, and monitor its output. For each stage you’ll practice with short examples: a file-existence check, a case driven menu for service control, a for loop that processes log files, a while loop that reads input, a small function that returns status, and a cron entry for nightly archiving. This progression builds practical skills you can use immediately in systems work and reduces common failures caused by unchecked errors or poor scheduling practices.

Conditional statements let your script make decisions based on file properties, string contents, numeric comparisons, or the exit status of commands. The basic if structure reads a condition and runs the then-block when the condition is true. Use the single-bracket form with spaces: open square bracket, condition, close square bracket. For richer pattern matching and logical operators prefer double square brackets. Typical tests include file checks like -f and -d, string tests such as -z for empty or == for equality, and numeric comparisons using -eq, -ne, -lt and so on. A practical example: test whether a configuration file exists and, if not, create a default one and report the action. A common mistake is leaving out spaces around brackets or using = for numeric comparisons; those errors either produce syntax errors or incorrect results. You can also combine conditions using && for AND and || for OR inside double brackets, or chain tests with elif to express multiple branches. When checking a command that returns success or failure, a compact pattern is to negate the command with an exclamation mark so the condition becomes true on non-zero exit status. To check your understanding, try writing a conditional that verifies a directory is writable and prints an error if it is not. The core idea is that correct spacing, operator choice, and thought about command exit behavior are what make conditionals reliable.

The case statement provides a concise and readable way to select one action from many possible values. Instead of chaining many elif conditions, case compares a variable against several patterns and executes the commands for the first matching pattern. Patterns can include simple words or shell globs such as start|stop|restart. Always end each pattern block with a double semicolon to separate it from the next. Use an asterisk star pattern as the default branch, similar to else. A common use is processing command-line arguments where the user passes a verb like start, stop or restart; case keeps the logic clear and avoids repetitive string comparisons. For example, a service-control script can map start to systemctl start and restart to systemctl restart. A misconception is thinking case matches substrings — it matches patterns, so include anchors or globs as needed. Also remember to quote variables where expansions may be empty. After building a case-based menu, test unexpected inputs to ensure the default branch handles mistakes gracefully. Consider pairing case with functions so each branch calls a named function, improving readability and testability.

A for loop iterates over a set of items and runs the same commands for each item. This is ideal for processing files, applying transformations, or batching administrative tasks. The basic pattern iterates over words or glob expansions: for FILE in *. log; do process "$FILE"; done. When filenames include spaces, quote variables to preserve the name as a single item. You can also iterate over a numeric sequence using brace expansion or seq. A common example is compressing all rotated logs or changing ownership across many files. For loops are deterministic: the list is evaluated before the loop runs, so adding or removing files during iteration may not affect the current pass. A typical mistake is using for FILE in $(ls *. log) which breaks on whitespace; prefer globs or an array. Use continue to skip items and break to exit the loop early on a fatal condition. For clarity and reuse, factor the per-item work into a function and call it from inside the loop. That makes debugging easier and lets you test the action independently of the looping mechanism.

While loops run as long as a given condition evaluates to true. They are suited for reading streams, waiting for a condition, or processing input until an end-of-file. A common idiom reads lines from a file safely with IFS read -r inside a while loop and then redirects the file into the loop. This avoids subshell issues and preserves whitespace. For example: while IFS= read -r LINE; do echo "$LINE"; done < input. txt. Another pattern uses a boolean condition that checks command output or the existence of a file, updating state inside the loop until the condition becomes false. The primary risk with while loops is infinite loops if the condition never changes; always ensure loop progress or include a timeout counter. To stop early on error, check exit status inside the loop and break if necessary. A misconception is expecting while to be faster than for — performance depends on the work done inside the loop. Design your loop body to do minimal external calls when processing many items to keep it efficient. while Loops means ensure the loop condition progresses, prefer ifs read -r for line input, and add timeouts or counters to prevent infinite loops.. In practical terms, repeat until a condition changes or input ends. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Functions let you group related commands into a named block that you can call with arguments. They make scripts easier to read and maintain, because you move repeated logic into a single place and give it a meaningful name. Define a function with function_name() { commands; } and call it by name. Inside the function use positional parameters like dollar sign one and dollar sign two to access passed arguments. Good practice is to return an exit status with return so callers can react based on success or failure. For example, create a function archive_file that takes a path, checks existence, appends it to the archive and returns non-zero on failure. This lets the main script call archive_file inside a loop and skip or retry on failure based on the returned status. A common misconception is that functions create a separate scope for variables — in POSIX shells, functions inherit and share the environment unless you explicitly use local to limit scope. Use local for temporary variables inside functions to avoid unintended side effects. Designing small, single-purpose functions improves testability and reduces the chance of bugs in large scripts.

Every command in a shell returns an exit status: zero typically means success, and any non-zero value signals an error. Scripts should check these statuses to decide how to proceed. The special variable dollar sign question holds the exit status of the most recently executed command. A practical pattern is to test the return value immediately after a critical command and take action on failure, such as retrying, logging, or exiting with a clear status. For instance, after attempting to create an archive you might test dollar sign question and print an error and exit with a non-zero code if archiving failed. Another common approach is to write functions that return specific codes for different failure modes, allowing higher-level logic to react appropriately. A misconception is assuming that a command printed to the terminal means it succeeded; always check the exit status. Also be aware that pipelines return the exit status of the last command in some shells by default; use pipefail if you need to detect failures earlier in a pipeline. Robust scripts explicitly handle errors near the source and provide informative messages so scheduled jobs don't silently fail.

The set -e option causes a script to exit immediately when a command returns a non-zero status. This is a useful safety mechanism for preventing later commands from running after an earlier failure. Use it at the top of scripts that should not continue when a step has failed. However, set -e has caveats: it may exit in contexts you expect to handle errors, such as conditional checks whose failures are used deliberately. You can work around this by checking command status explicitly when you expect non-zero outcomes, or by using command lists with || true for tolerated failures. Another helpful option for pipelines is set -o pipefail which ensures the pipeline's exit status reflects the first failing command instead of the last. A common misconception is that set -e alone makes a script fully robust — it helps, but you still need explicit checks and clear return codes in functions. Test scripts with intentional failures to understand how set -e affects control flow. When combined with good logging and return codes, set -e reduces the risk of scripts continuing in a broken state and causing wider system issues.

We'll walk through a practical script that archives log files older than seven days and then schedule it with cron. The script starts with a shebang and set -e to enforce fail-fast behavior. It defines variables for the log and archive directories and ensures the archive directory exists. It then finds matching files older than seven days using find with -mtime +7 and writes the list to a temporary file. If the list is non-empty, the script creates a compressed archive with tar and removes originals, logging progress as it goes. Note the use of checks for directory existence and testing whether the temp file is empty to avoid running tar on an empty list. After testing locally, schedule the script using crontab -e. A correct crontab entry for daily 2:00 AM uses minute hour day month weekday fields: 0 2 * * * followed by the absolute script path and redirected output to a log file. For testing, schedule the job a minute or two in the future to confirm it runs and writes expected output. Common mistakes are forgetting full paths in cron or not redirecting stdout and stderr, which can lead to unexpected mailbox messages. This exercise ties conditionals, loops, functions and cron into a single, verifiable workflow.

These are the core concepts to retain. First, conditional statements let scripts branch based on tests like file checks, string emptiness, or numeric comparison; remember proper spacing and operator choices. Second, use the case statement for multiple distinct choices to keep the logic clear and maintainable. Third, for and while loops let you automate repetitive work: prefer globs and quoted variables in for loops and use IFS read -r for safe line-by-line processing. Fourth, functions modularize code, accept parameters, use local variables to avoid side effects, and return exit codes so callers can handle outcomes appropriately. Fifth, every command returns an exit status accessible via $?: check it to detect and respond to failures. Sixth, set -e helps scripts fail fast but requires deliberate handling for expected non-zero outcomes. Finally, cron schedules jobs reliably when you use absolute paths and redirect output. These elements together let you write maintainable, robust scripts and automate routine tasks with confidence.

Keep these quick reminders handy as you write scripts. First, test expressions carefully: use the right operators and spacing and prefer double brackets for complex logic. Second, modularize work in functions and return meaningful exit statuses so higher-level logic can respond accurately. Third, schedule carefully with cron using the script’s absolute path and redirect both stdout and stderr so you can inspect logs and avoid surprising emails. These three practices—correct tests, modular functions with clear return codes, and mindful scheduling—prevent most common failures in scripted automation. When you combine them with set -e and pipefail where appropriate, your scripts become predictable and easier to support. Before you finish, run the archive script manually, check the archive contents, and test the crontab for a quick run to confirm behavior. That small habit turns a good script into a reliable automation tool.
